Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 102, verse 1–4:

Page 519
﴿Rivalry in worldly gain distracts you﴾ [1] ﴿until you visit the graves﴾ [2] ﴿No! You will come to know﴾ [3] ﴿Then, no! You will come to know﴾ [4].

(Alhakum) means: it preoccupied you with what it is incumbent upon you to be preoccupied with, because distraction (lahw) is a preoccupation that diverts one from attaining an important matter.

And al-takathur (mutual rivalry in multiplying) is a form of tafa'ul derived from kuthr, meaning the competing in increasing something that is desired in its abundance. Of it is rivalry in wealth, and of it is rivalry in number, of children and allies, for the sake of pride in them. The verse has been interpreted as including both. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They said, "We have more wealth and children, and we will not be punished."﴾ [Saba': 35].

And al-A'sha said:

You are not the most numerous of them in pebbles, but glory belongs to the one who is most numerous.

Muslim narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Shikhkhir, who said: "I came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ while he was reciting (Alhakum al-takathur), and he said: 'The son of Adam says: my wealth, my wealth. And do you have, O son of Adam, of your wealth anything except what you eat and so consume, or what you wear and so wear out, or what you give in charity and so send ahead?'" This serves as an explanation of one of the meanings of takathur, which the situation of the admonition at that moment required and which the verse necessitates.

The address is to the polytheists, as indicated by the severity of the threat in His saying: ﴿No! You will come to know. Then, no! You will come to know﴾, and His saying: ﴿You will surely see the Hellfire﴾ [al-Takathur: 6] to the end of the surah, and because this is not the character of the Muslims at that time.

The intended addressees are their chiefs and the wealthy among them, due to His saying: ﴿Then you will surely be questioned that Day about pleasure﴾ [al-Takathur: 8], and because the chiefs of the polytheists are those who preferred the blessing they were in over being keen to receive the call of the Prophet ﷺ, so they stood against his denial and incited the masses not to listen to him. Therefore the thing one is distracted from is not mentioned, since it is evident that it is the Qur'an, reflecting upon it, and acknowledging its truth. This distraction occurred from them and was realized, as indicated by its narration in the past tense.

And if the address is to the polytheists, then it is because the Muslims know that being engaged in this sort of character is blameworthy in the sight of Allah, and that it is among the traits of the people of shirk, so they know they are warned against being engaged in any of that, and they are wary lest love of wealth distract them from some act of good, and they anticipate that death may overtake them while they are heedless of goodness. Allah the Exalted says, addressing the believers: ﴿Know that the life of this world is but play and amusement and adornment and boasting among yourselves and rivalry in wealth and children, like the rain whose vegetation pleases the disbelievers﴾ [al-Hadid: 20], to the end of the verse.

His saying: ﴿until you visit the graves﴾ is a limit (ghayah). It may be a limit for the verb (alhakum), as in His saying the Exalted: ﴿They said, "We will not cease to be devoted to it until Moses returns to us"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 91], meaning: the distraction of rivalry continued until you visited the graves, that is, it persisted with you throughout your lives. So the limit is used to encompass the times of what is limited, not to end it and bring about its opposite, because when they reach the graves, all their deeds are cut off.

Because visiting graves in this sense is an expression for dwelling in them, that is, the graves of the cemeteries. The real meaning of ziyarah is to be present in a place without remaining there permanently, so the verb ziyarah is used here as an implicit reproach to them, that their dwelling in the graves is followed by departure from them.

The use of the past tense in (zurtum) is to place the future in the position of the past, because its occurrence is certain, like His saying: ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ [al-Nahl: 1].

It is also possible that the limit belongs to what is being multiplied by, which is indicated by takathur, that is, with everything, even with the graves that you prepare. This accords with what Muqatil and al-Kalbi narrated, that the Banu 'Abd Manaf and the Banu Sahm boasted of the abundance of their chiefs among them, as was mentioned earlier concerning the occasion of its revelation. Then the visiting is used in its literal meaning, that is, you visited the graves in order to count the graves. The Arabs use the grave as a kinaya (metonymy) for its occupant. al-Nabigha said:

If there is for the two graves a grave in Jillaq, and a grave at Saida' which is near Harib...

And 'Isam ibn 'Ubayd al-Zimmani, or Hammam al-Raqashi, said:

If a grave and a grave were counted, I would be the nearest of them to you in grave, and the farthest of them from the abode of the blamer.

That is: I would be the nearest of them to you in grave, that is, the owner of a grave.

Page 521
Al-maqabir is the plural of maqbarah, with fath or damm on the ba'. Al-maqbarah is the land in which there are many graves.

The rebuke in which the statement is used is followed by a threat of punishment after death, and by the particle of restraint and nullification in His saying: ﴿No! You will come to know﴾. So (kalla) conveys restraint and nullification of the rivalry.

And (sawfa) is for affirming the occurrence of knowledge. The object of (ta'lamun) is omitted because it is evident that what is meant is: you will come to know the evil outcome of your heedlessness through rivalry, in turning away from accepting the call of Islam.

The restraint and threat are emphasized by His saying: ﴿Then, no! You will come to know﴾, so it is conjoined by a verbal conjunction with the particle of delay as well, to indicate that the rank of this restraint and threat is distant from the rank of the restraint and threat before it. So this is a restraint and threat similar to the first, but its conjunction with (thumma) requires it to be stronger than the first, because it affirms the first and magnifies it.

Thus the clause ﴿Then, no! You will come to know﴾ is a verbal emphasis of the clause ﴿No! You will come to know﴾. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿No! You will come to know﴾ refers to the punishment that will befall you in the grave; ﴿Then, no! You will come to know﴾ refers to at the Resurrection, that what you were promised is true. That is, each clause is taken to mean a threat with a specific thing. This is among the consequences of the structures and of relying on the aid of context, by supposing a specific object for each of the two verbs (ta'lamun), and the repetition of the clause does not necessarily require that in the original speech, though the effect of repetition is achieved in every case.

Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah 102, verse 5:

﴿Nay, were you to know with the knowledge of certainty!﴾

The warning is repeated a third time, to add to the nullification of what they are engaged in: the distraction from reflecting on the words of the Qur'an. The hope is that they will desist from their absorption in multiplying (*al-takathur*), in what they are multiplying, and in their diversion through it from considering the call to the truth and to monotheism. The object of (*ta'lamun*, "you know") is omitted for the reason already mentioned under ﴿Nay, you will soon know﴾ [al-Takathur: 3]. The apodosis of (*law*, "if/were") is also omitted.

The clause ﴿were you to know with the knowledge of certainty﴾ is intended to alarm and shock, because omitting the apodosis of (*law*) leaves the mind to imagine every possible outcome. The meaning is: if you knew with the knowledge of certainty, there would become clear to you a terrible and enormous state of affairs. This clause explains the warning contained in (*kalla*, "nay").

The imperfect verb in ﴿were you to know﴾ refers to the present time. That is, if you knew now with the knowledge of certainty, you would know a great matter.

The conditional verb after (*law*) has many states and considerations. It may occur in the perfect form or in the imperfect form, and in both it may be used in its literal meaning. It may also be used in a meaning other than its literal one. Here it is used in its literal meaning, referring to the present, without any transference or interpretation.

The genitive construction (*'ilm*, "knowledge") with (*al-yaqin*, "certainty") is an explicative (*bayaniyyah*) annexation, since certainty is itself a form of knowledge. That is: if you knew with knowledge that corresponds to reality, the abhorrent nature of what you are engaged in would become evident to you. But their knowledge of their own circumstances is ignorance compounded of illusions and fancies. In this there is a rebuke for them for their failure to acquire sound knowledge. This address is directed at the polytheists who do not believe in recompense, not at the Muslims, because the Muslims already know this with the knowledge of certainty.

Know that this compound, *'ilm al-yaqin* (knowledge of certainty), was transferred into technical scholarly usage and became a title for a state of what the intellect apprehends. Its explanation has already been given in the commentary on the words of the Exalted: ﴿And indeed it is the truth of certainty﴾ [al-Haqqah: 51] in Surah al-Haqqah, so refer back to it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 102, verses 6–7:

﴿You will surely see the Blazing Fire﴾ ﴿Then you will surely see it with the eye of certainty﴾

This is a resumptive explanatory sentence (*isti'naf bayani*, a sentence that answers an implied question). The preceding repeated warning and rebuke, and the emphatic threat, which are general in their wording, stir in the listener's soul a question about what is awaited from this warning and threat. So His saying ﴿You will surely see the Blazing Fire﴾ is the answer to what stirs within the listener's soul.

His saying ﴿You will surely see the Blazing Fire﴾ is not the answer (*jawab*) of "law" (*law*, "if") in the sense of "if you knew with certainty you would be like those who see the Blazing Fire," meaning "you would surely see it with your hearts." This is because the structure of the speech is that of an oath, as shown by its being joined with the emphatic *nun* (*nun al-tawkid*). Therefore this *lam* is not the *lam* of the answer of "law," because the answer of "law" is one whose occurrence is impossible, and so the emphatic *nun* does not attach to it.

The report about their seeing the Blazing Fire is a metonymy (*kinaya*) for entering into it, since entering into a thing necessitates seeing it. So seeing is used as a metonymy for presence, as in the saying of Ja'far ibn 'Ulba al-Harithi:

Page 523

*None removes the great distress except the son of a free woman,*
*who sees the waves of death and then visits them.*

This is emphasized by His saying ﴿Then you will surely see it with the eye of certainty﴾, intended to confirm the threat in its metonymic meaning. This emphasis is joined by *thumma* ("then"), which here expresses gradation in rank (*al-tarakhi al-rutbi*), in the same manner as we established just before in His saying ﴿Then nay, you will soon know﴾ [al-Takathur: 4]. There are not two sightings, one occurring after the other with an interval.

"'Ayn al-yaqin" (the eye of certainty): the certainty that is not mixed with any doubt. The word *'ayn* is a figurative use (*majaz*) for the pure reality of a thing, which is neither deficient nor merely similar.

The genitive construction of *'ayn* with *al-yaqin* is an explicative genitive (*idafa bayaniyya*), like the genitive of *haqq* with *al-yaqin* in His saying ﴿Indeed, this is the true certainty﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 95].

The majority of reciters read ﴿You will surely see the Blazing Fire﴾ with an opening *ta'* (*bi-fath al-muthannat al-fawqiyya*). Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read it with a *ḍamma* on the *ta'* from *ara(hu)* (causative form).

As for ﴿la-tarawunnaha﴾ ("you will surely see it"), the reciters did not differ in reading it with an opening *ta'*.

In al-Kashshaf, it is indicated that these verses, which begin with His saying ﴿Nay, you will soon know﴾ [al-Takathur: 3] and end with His saying ﴿the eye of certainty﴾, contain several aspects of strengthening the warning and rebuke. It begins with the particle of rebuke and warning, and after it comes the particle *thumma*, which indicates that the second warning is more eloquent than the first. The particle of rebuke and warning is repeated, and the answer of ﴿if you knew﴾ [al-Takathur: 5] is omitted, because omitting it carries an exaggeration of awe. The oath particle *lam* is brought to emphasize the threat. This oath is further emphasized by another oath. These are six aspects.

I say, in addition to that: in His saying ﴿the eye of certainty﴾ there are two emphases on the seeing, in that it is certainty, and that certainty is a reality. What is said about the genitive construction of ﴿the eye of certainty﴾ is the same as what is said about the genitive construction of ﴿the knowledge of certainty﴾ [al-Takathur: 5], mentioned just before.

[Page 524]

﴿Then you will surely be questioned that Day about the bliss.﴾

Having censured and threatened them for their preoccupation with mutual rivalry in piling up wealth (al-takathur), he turned away from considering the call to Islam, in that this rivalry prevented them from accepting what would save them. The verse threatens and warns them that they will be called to account for the bliss they enjoyed in this world without giving thanks to God for it, through His saying: ﴿Then you will surely be questioned that Day about the bliss﴾. That is, about the bliss that was bestowed upon you in this world, for which you did not thank God, and which was the cause of your insolence (baṭar).

This statement is joined with the particle (thumma, "then"), which indicates a gradual elevation in rank (al-tarākhī al-rutbī) in its coordination of sentences. This is because the reckoning concerning bliss, which is a favour from God, is more severe for them, since they did not expect it. Their adherence to polytheism while enjoying bliss is a greater ingratitude toward the One who bestowed favours upon them.

Al-naʿīm (bliss) is a term for what a person finds pleasant and which is not constant for him. Thus health, the soundness of the senses, the soundness of perception, sleep and wakefulness are not among the bliss, whereas drinking water, eating food, delighting in what is heard, in what brings pride, and in seeing beautiful things are counted as bliss.

Al-naʿīm is more specific than al-niʿmah (favour) with a kasra on the nūn, and is synonymous with al-niʿmah with a fatḥa on the nūn.

Al-naʿīm was discussed previously at His saying: ﴿For them therein is lasting bliss﴾ [al-Tawbah: 21], in Surah Barāʾah (al-Tawbah).

The address is directed to the polytheists, in keeping with the pattern of the preceding addresses.

The clause to which (idh) is annexed in His saying (yawmaʾidhin, "that Day") is elided, and it is indicated by His saying: ﴿You will surely see the Hellfire﴾ [al-Takāthur: 6]. That is: on the Day when you see the Hellfire, the punishment will become severe upon you.

This questioning about bliss directed at the polytheists is different from the questioning that every person who has been favoured will undergo regarding how he spent the favour. Since favour was not exclusive to the polytheists, unlike rivalry in accumulation, questioning about it is fitting for every person favoured, although the states of the recompense that results from this questioning differ.

This is supported by what is related in the ḥadīth of Muslim from Abū Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out one day, and found Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, and they got up with him. He came to a man of the Anṣār, but he was not in his house. Then the Anṣārī came, looked at the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his two companions, and said: 'Praise be to God, no one today has a more honourable guest than me.' So he went and brought them a bunch of dates containing unripe, ripe and fully ripened dates, took a knife and slaughtered a sheep for them. They ate from the sheep and from that bunch and drank. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: 'By Him in whose hand my soul is, you will surely be questioned about the bliss of this day on the Day of Resurrection.'" [The hadith continues.] This is a questioning about bliss established by the Sunnah (the practice of the Prophet, ﷺ), and it is other than the one mentioned in this verse.

The Anṣārī was Abū al-Haytham ibn al-Tayyihān, whose name was Mālik.

The meaning of the ḥadīth is: "you will surely be questioned about giving thanks for that favour." He intended to remind them to give thanks for every favour. The questioning of believers is a questioning in order to arrange the reward for gratitude, or for the purpose of being held accountable for forbidden bliss.

Al-Qurṭubī mentioned: "From al-Ḥasan: Only the people of the Fire will be questioned about bliss." It is also narrated that when this verse was revealed, Abū Bakr said: "O Messenger of God, what do you think of a meal I ate with you in the house of Abū al-Haytham ibn al-Tayyihān, of barley bread, meat and unripe dates that were hot and not sweet? Do we fear that this is among the bliss about which we will be questioned?" He (ʿalayhi al-salām) said: "That is for the disbelievers," and then he recited: ﴿And do We requite any but the ungrateful?﴾ [Saba': 17].

Al-Qushayrī said: "The reconciliation between the reports is that all will be questioned, but the questioning of the disbeliever is a questioning of rebuke, because he abandoned gratitude, while the questioning of the believer is a questioning of honour, because he gave thanks."

The clause to which (idh) is annexed in His saying (yawmaʾidhin, "that Day") is elided, and it is indicated by His saying: ﴿You will surely see the Hellfire﴾ [al-Takāthur: 6]. That is: on the Day when you see the Hellfire, so the punishment will become severe upon you.

Surah al-ʿAṣr (The Declining Day)

Ibn Kathīr mentioned that al-Ṭabarānī narrated with his chain of transmission from ʿUbayd Allāh ibn Ḥuṣayn, who said: "When two of the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) met, they would not part until one of them recited to the other Surah al-ʿAṣr, etc., as will follow."

This is likewise its name in many copies of the Qur'an and in most books of tafsir (exegesis). It is also so in an ancient copy in the Kufic script among the Qayrawānī copies from the fifth century.

In some books of tafsir and in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī it is called (Surah wa-al-ʿAṣr), with the wāw retained, in quotation of the first word in it; that is, "the surah of this word."

It is Meccan according to the majority, and this is the general view of most exegetes. From Qatādah, Mujāhid and Muqātil it is related that it is Medinan. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, and the author of al-Itqān did not include it among the surahs whose status is disputed.

It is counted as the thirteenth in the order of the revelation of the surahs. It was revealed after Surah al-Inshirāḥ and before Surah al-ʿĀdiyāt.

Its verses number three.

It is one of three surahs which are the shortest in number of verses: it, al-Kawthar, and Surah al-Naṣr.

* * *

It includes the affirmation of severe loss for the people of polytheism and those who are like them among the people of disbelief in Islam after its call has been delivered; likewise for whoever takes up the works of falsehood against which Islam warned the Muslims.

It includes the affirmation of the salvation and success of those who believed and did righteous deeds, and of those among them who called to the truth.

It includes the excellence of patience in purifying the soul and in calling to the truth.

The Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) took it as their emblem when they met. Al-Ṭabarānī narrated with his chain to ʿUbayd Allāh ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Ḥuṣayn al-Anṣārī, one of the Successors (al-tābiʿūn), that he said: "When two of the Companions of the Messenger of God met, they would not part until one of them recited to the other Surah al-ʿAṣr to its end, and then one of them would give the salām to the other, that is, the salām of parting. This is also a Sunnah, like the salām of arrival."

From al-Shāfiʿī: "If people reflected upon this surah, it would suffice them." In another report from him: "If nothing had been revealed to people except it, it would have been enough for them." Others said: "It encompasses all the sciences of the Qur'an." Its explanation will come later.
